name: Neck training harness
lead: A neck training harness is a head strap or cap, connected by a chain or strap to a weight plate or resistance, that loads the neck muscles through flexion, extension and side flexion. Wrestlers, boxers and other combat-sport athletes have long used neck strengthening, and the harness has been adopted by people who want a thicker neck for appearance reasons, since neck size changes how the head and jaw sit against the shoulders in photographs and on camera.

No review located for this article focuses on neck muscle size in healthy recreational lifters, so the appearance claim rests mainly on general principles of resistance training. The surrounding research covers neck exercise in people with neck pain, in athletes where neck strength is studied as a way to reduce head acceleration events, and in healthy volunteers in small trials of strength and muscle cross-sectional area.[1][2][3][4]

paras: Harnesses generally consist of a padded leather or nylon cap or strap that fits around the head, with a chain or strap that attaches to a weight plate or dumbbell. Some versions combine a head strap with a chin cup, and variants use resistance bands or a partner's hands. A user lies on a bench or sits and moves the head against the load.

Neck muscles are skeletal muscles, and the working assumption in strength training is that they adapt to progressive loading, adequate volume and recovery as other muscles do. A 2008 electromyographic study compared neck conditioning exercises in healthy controls,[5] and a 2013 randomised pilot trial in 26 healthy women compared two ten-week neck-training programmes, one with resistance training and one combining resistance with proprioceptive work, assessing neck strength and the cross-sectional area of three neck muscle groups.[3]

Training can also change how the nervous system controls the neck. A 2013 trial in Spine found sustained increases in corticomotor excitability, measured with transcranial magnetic stimulation, after specific neck training.[4]

A randomised trial of 180 women with chronic neck pain compared high-intensity strength training and endurance training with a control group over a year of follow-up, with greatest strength gains reported in the training groups.[6] A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis in PLOS ONE examined effects of exercise on neuromuscular function in people with chronic neck pain.[7] Reviews of deep cervical flexor training have likewise examined impaired physiological function in chronic neck pain.[8]

The 2013 pilot trial measured muscle cross-sectional area in healthy women after ten weeks, but the evidence base for visible neck thickening in healthy male and female lifters is small and indirect.[3] Proponents describe visibly thicker necks after months of training; no controlled trial cited in this article tests the claim of an altered facial or jaw profile.

A 2025 systematic review and Delphi consensus in the British Journal of Sports Medicine examined neck training in sport to reduce head acceleration events and developed expert consensus on how it should be implemented.[1] A 2025 review of head acceleration in soccer headers and a 2026 review of concussion prevention in adult football identified few studies of head-neck training.[2][9] A 2024 report in Cureus described concussion reduction in collegiate athletes after a simple cervical exercise regimen.[10]

The cervical spine contains the spinal cord, nerve roots and vertebral arteries, and heavy loads, jerky repetitions or poor control are generally described as raising the risk of muscle strain and nerve irritation. Training guidance commonly advises starting with very light resistance and progressing gradually. People with prior neck injury, disc problems or dizziness are generally advised to consult a clinician before loading the neck. These precautions come from general clinical practice and not from trials of the harness.

In appearance and physique communities neck training is presented as a way to broaden the neck, which proponents say balances the head and improves the look of the jaw, shoulders and traps in profile and on camera. The harness is described as an inexpensive route to progressive overload compared with machine-based neck equipment.

Typical points compared between products are padding and fit of the head cap, strap or chain length, the weight-bearing attachment point and whether the strap is adjustable for head size. Prices commonly fall in the range of about $20 to $40.

No studies found testing the harness itself. Research on neck training in general includes a randomised pilot trial of neck resistance training in 26 healthy women measuring strength and muscle cross-sectional area,[3] a 180-woman trial of strength versus endurance neck training in chronic neck pain,[6] a trial of neck training and corticomotor excitability,[4] a meta-analysis of exercise and neuromuscular function in chronic neck pain,[7] and sports reviews of neck training to reduce head acceleration events.[1][2][9]

lore.intro: Neck training is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, where users discuss it as a way to build a thicker neck that they say complements the jaw and physique, and share routines and results [11][12].

claims.claim: A thicker, stronger neck improves physique, posture and a 'high T' look
claims.believers: A looksmax.org guide says a thicker and stronger neck goes hand in hand with the physique, helps posture over time and makes one look like a 'high T mogger'; it recommends neck extension and flexion exercises with a towel over the head [12].
claims.experts: Studies in the sources reviewed here measured neck strength, muscle cross-sectional area and electromyographic activity, and training for neck pain or head-impact reduction; none assessed perceived attractiveness or hormonal appearance [3][5][6][1]. A randomized trial in healthy women compared two ten-week neck programs for strength and muscle cross-sectional area [3].

claims.claim: Neck exercises can be done without added weight if done slowly with a stretch
claims.believers: A reply in the guide thread says one does not even need weight if training slowly and prioritising stretch, which should aid hypertrophy; another adds tension and reps with good technique [12].
claims.experts: Published neck-training studies used resistance, isometric or proprioceptive protocols; no study in the sources reviewed here tested slow bodyweight neck work for hypertrophy [3][5][6].

claims.claim: Training the neck three times a week for two months should show visible results
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user reports training his neck about three times weekly for two months and seeing no results, and asks whether his routine is wrong [11].
claims.experts: A ten-week trial in healthy women measured neck strength and muscle cross-sectional area after twice-weekly training [3]. A randomized trial in women with chronic neck pain reported strength gains over high- and low-intensity programs [6].
